history.contentIn: The Stratospheric Controlled Perturbation Experiment (SCoPEx) was an initiative by Harvard University aimed at advancing our understanding of aerosol behavior in the stratosphere. This scientific endeavor, led by Frank Keutsch and his collaborators, was intended to refine computer models that assess the risks and benefits of solar geoengineering—not to implement geoengineering itself or to cool the planet. The proposed experiment involved a scientific balloon gondola operating at high altitudes, releasing a minuscule amount of calcium carbonate for measurement purposes. Importantly, a 2021 platform test in Sweden was focused solely on hardware, with the SCoPEx Advisory Committee advocating for a pause pending societal engagement, ensuring transparency and public accountability. As of March 2024, Harvard announced that the project would no longer be pursued, redirecting the platform towards research that prioritizes scientific integrity and climate justice without resorting to unverified geoengineering methods. history.contentIn: Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) is a proposed solar radiation modification method that would introduce aerosols into the stratosphere to reflect a small fraction of incoming sunlight, analogous in mechanism to cooling after large volcanic eruptions such as Mount Pinatubo in 1991. The IPCC has described SAI as the most-researched solar geoengineering approach and notes that, used at moderate intensity, it could limit warming, but imperfectly and with other possible effects if used suboptimally. Candidate materials discussed in the literature include sulfates and, in some proposals, calcite or other particles. Delivery concepts include specialised high-altitude aircraft; there is no operational global SAI deployment. SAI would not remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, would not stop ocean acidification, and would require a sustained commitment if used to offset continued high emissions. Risks discussed in assessments include ozone chemistry, changes in precipitation patterns, termination shock if a program stopped abruptly, and governance problems. Small research proposals such as Harvard's SCoPEx aimed to measure aerosol microphysics in a tiny plume, not to cool the planet. Public claims that routine commercial aviation is already injecting SAI materials as 'chemtrails' are not supported by atmospheric science.

history.contentIn: Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) depend on sea ice as a platform for hunting seals. Arctic sea ice has declined in extent and thickness over the satellite era as the Arctic has warmed about twice as fast as the global mean (Arctic amplification). The IUCN and Arctic scientists treat loss of sea-ice hunting habitat as the primary long-term threat to the species. Some subpopulations have been relatively stable or better counted in recent surveys, which deniers sometimes quote as 'polar bears are fine.' That snapshot does not cancel the physical dependence on ice or projections of increased fasting and reduced cub survival as ice-free seasons lengthen, especially in southern parts of the range. Polar-bear numbers are not a single global census with low error; management units differ. Conservation hunting quotas and pollution are additional pressures, but they do not make sea-ice loss irrelevant. There is no scientific basis for the claim that polar bears are thriving because of chemtrails or that global warming is a hoax because one subpopulation increased.
